Kadalundi Technologies: The Week That Runs the Company

Delivery & Technology · Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

1. Sunday night, Kakkanad

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 13 September 2026, Devika Menon was still at the dining table of her Kakkanad flat, three kilometres from the Infopark campus where Kadalundi Technologies occupied two and a half floors. Four printouts lay before her: a delivery dashboard, a customer-success escalation log, an engagement-survey summary, and a one-page extract from the share purchase agreement under which Kadalundi had bought a Pune company two years earlier. Menon, Chief Product and Technology Officer, had read them in rotation all weekend, and the more carefully she read them the less they agreed with one another.

On Monday at nine, in the all-hands the company had held weekly for four years, she was expected to say something about the way Kadalundi worked. On Thursday, 17 September, she would sit before a board already told, in a deck she approved in July, that the company ran "a disciplined weekly delivery rhythm across all four product pods." She no longer believed that sentence, and was not certain it had been true when she approved it. What she could not decide was whether the rhythm had broken, had never been the thing holding the company together, or was working exactly as designed and had been quietly captured by the people it was meant to hold to account.

Her phone had buzzed twice. Priyam Sarkar, from a working afternoon in Toronto: "The incident numbers in the board pack — there's a definitions thing you should know before Thursday." Then Rohit Dandekar in Pune: "Heard about Monday. Before you announce anything, please call me." Menon had answered neither.

2. The company, and a signature that still binds it

Kadalundi Technologies Private Limited was founded in Kochi in 2018 by Ashwin Kurup, a former Infosys healthcare-practice architect, and two colleagues who had spent a decade watching Indian hospitals lose money between treating a patient and being paid. Their first product, Kadalundi Claims, assembled insurance claims out of a hospital's own messy records: discharge summaries, pharmacy line items, implant invoices, tariff tables that differed for every payer. It sold well in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and then Maharashtra because it moved a number finance heads cared about: days from discharge to cash.

The second product, Kadalundi Connect, was the consequential one. Built from 2021, it let a hospital group talk to twenty-odd insurers and third-party administrators through one interface, later through the National Health Claims Exchange. Connect turned Kadalundi from a departmental tool into plumbing, and plumbing has a different customer: large, slow, contractual, unforgiving about downtime. By September 2026 the company had 143 people in product and engineering, ₹196 crore of annualised revenue, and customers including Ashtamudi Hospitals, a 2,100-bed chain across Kerala and coastal Karnataka, and Zawiya Medical Group of Dubai, worth ₹9.4 crore a year on its own.

The decision that constrained Menon's Monday had been taken in March 2024, when Kadalundi acquired Tarangini Software Labs, a 38-person Pune firm with a fast, well-regarded claims-adjudication engine. Tarangini's founders were reluctant sellers. To close, Kurup agreed to an earn-out to 31 March 2027 worth up to ₹47 crore and — at Tarangini's insistence, against counsel's advice — to a clause guaranteeing "the continued operational and engineering autonomy of the acquired unit, including its own release, planning and review practices" for that period. In 2024 that had looked like a sentimental concession to a proud founding team. In September 2026 it meant the largest engineering group in the company, 51 people under Rohit Dandekar in Pune, could not lawfully be instructed to attend Menon's meetings.

3. The industry around it

Indian health claims in 2026 were being rewired by policy faster than by competition. The National Health Authority's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had established identifiers and registries; the National Health Claims Exchange had moved from pilot to production, and a payer consortium had set a target of 1 January 2027 for hospital networks to exchange claims over it in standard form. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had brought consent managers and breach-notification timelines to a sector that had moved patient data by email and scanned PDF. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India was pressing insurers on cashless settlement turnaround, and that pressure travelled down the chain.

The competitive map was crowded but uneven. Infosys, TCS and Wipro bid for the same hospital groups with integration programmes measured in crores and quarters. Newer health-tech firms and the technology arms of payers such as Star Health, Niva Bupa and HDFC Ergo built adjacent pieces; Practo and the chains' own IT teams held the front end. Kadalundi's ground was narrow: faster than the services firms, deeper in claims than the startups, further along on NHCX than either. That advantage had a shelf life measured in quarters.

The Gulf exposure changed the arithmetic again. Zawiya Medical Group had signed in 2023 on terms Kadalundi's sales head called "the price of credibility": named release windows on the first Sunday of each quarter, a ten-working-day change freeze either side, service credits of ₹18 lakh per severity-one breach capped at eight per cent of contract value, and a written change notice to Zawiya's IT governance committee every Thursday. Zawiya's board was now evaluating a five-year regional platform contract worth a possible ₹40 crore a year. Dubai ran Sunday to Thursday; Kochi ran Monday to Friday; the overlap with Toronto was ninety minutes on a good day and none on Friday.

4. What happened, what was believed, and what has since proved wrong

The weekly rhythm was Menon's own initiative, and for most of 2026 she had counted it among the better things she had done. She had joined in September 2025 from a Bengaluru software firm, into an organisation that shipped when it felt ready and reviewed when something went wrong. In November 2025 a botched pharmacy-tariff change cost Ashtamudi Hospitals eleven days of rejected claims; the post-mortem found three people had known the change was risky and none had had a place to say so. Her response, designed over the Christmas break with Karthika Ramanathan, was a calendar: a fifteen-minute daily standup per pod; a Wednesday metric check at 4 p.m. IST walking a fixed dashboard; a Thursday release review at 2 p.m. IST where each pod declared what was going out and the Zawiya change notice was assembled; and a rotating retrospective every second Friday.

It launched on 12 January 2026 with a memo and a calendar invitation, and for four months appeared to work. Deploy frequency rose, lead time fell, and dashboard incidents halved between January and July. Menon's July board slide said the rhythm had "reduced production incidents by 58 per cent." Ramanathan's team had built the slide; Menon had checked that the number matched the dashboard, which it did.

Three things had since turned out to be untrue, or at least unsafe.

The first concerned the numbers. In May 2026, following a well-intentioned effort to make severity grading consistent, the incident taxonomy was revised. Two categories — "partner-side" and "configuration drift" — were introduced and excluded from the production-incident count, on the grounds that they were not defects in Kadalundi's code. Between May and August, 23 incidents were classified into them, including four that took Connect's submission flow offline for Zawiya and two visible to Ashtamudi's billing floor for over an hour. On the dashboard, none of them existed. Exhibits 3 and 4 are the same eight months seen from inside and from outside.

The second concerned Pune. Dandekar's unit attended the Thursday release review reliably through March, intermittently through April and May, and stopped in June after a collision with its own Tuesday planning. Nobody escalated it: attendance was not tracked, and from Kochi, Pune's work still appeared on the release notes — generated from the Kochi Jira project, while Pune deployed from trunk several times a day and filed tickets afterwards for traceability. For eleven of the nineteen weeks between April and August, the change notice sent to Zawiya's governance committee listed items that had not yet shipped and omitted items that had.

The third concerned the Wednesday metric check, the part of the design Menon believed in most. Notes for the twenty-two sessions between February and August showed a median of zero action items and a median duration of twelve minutes against a scheduled forty-five. The dashboard was presented; questions were asked in perhaps a third of sessions; nothing was decided, because the people who could decide anything had drifted, without discussion, into treating Wednesday as a reporting slot and Thursday as the real meeting.

5. The people

Devika Menon, Chief Product and Technology Officer, Kochi. Menon owns the rhythm and, on Thursday, the board's view of it. She believes the real problem is that bad news has nowhere to land, but cannot say so without indicting a system she built and a number she signed. Her equity refresh is tied to the Series C opening diligence in October, and a story about broken delivery discipline does not help a round. She has told nobody, including Kurup, that she has drafted a board memo retracting the 58 per cent figure.

Ashwin Kurup, co-founder and Chief Executive, Kochi. Kurup's position is that the company is over-processed: "we had none of this when we were winning." He wants NHCX shipped, Zawiya renewed and the round closed, and treats cadence as an internal matter Menon should resolve. His incentive is the Series C valuation. He is not saying that two investors asked specifically about delivery predictability after speaking to a reference customer, and that he answered by quoting the July slide.

Karthika Ramanathan, Director of Delivery, Bengaluru. Ramanathan designed the rhythm's operational detail and runs it. She holds that the cadence is sound and enforcement weak: she wants attendance tracked, a Monday planning session added, participation written into every lead's objectives. Her role exists because the rhythm exists, and her April promotion case rests on the improvement the dashboard shows. She is not saying that she wrote the May taxonomy definitions herself, after a conversation in which Kurup asked her why the incident line "never seems to improve."

Rohit Dandekar, Vice President of Engineering, Pune, and co-founder of Tarangini. Dandekar holds that his unit's practices beat Kochi's and that the numbers support him: Pune has the lowest change failure rate in the company and does hold a daily standup, Tuesday planning and a genuine fortnightly retro. He does not attend Kochi's meetings, which he regards as reporting theatre. His incentive is the ₹47 crore earn-out, whose final tranche vests on 31 March 2027 against milestones that mention neither Zawiya nor NHCX. He is not saying that he has had two conversations with a Pune competitor, and that eleven of his 51 engineers vest when he does.

Priyam Sarkar, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Sarkar built and maintains the dashboard. He argues the weekly metric check measures the wrong things: deploy frequency and lead time describe the factory, not the customer, and the only honest number is one nobody looks at — claims that failed to reach a payer in the promised window. He wants the metrics rebuilt around customer-visible failure, and has a platform project he has pushed for a year. He is not quite saying that he noticed the reclassification in June, posted it to a thread that received no replies, and let it go; or that he has a second-round interview with a Toronto fintech on 22 September.

Johanna Reuter, Principal Designer, Berlin. Reuter covers both products across a four-and-a-half-hour time difference. She argues the rhythm crowded out the only ritual that mattered to quality — the ninety-minute design and engineering critique on alternate Wednesdays, folded into the metric check in February to save calendar space. She now runs an unofficial critique with two engineers and Sarkar at a time suiting Berlin and Toronto, unadvertised. She is not saying that she has twice asked to move to a four-day week and heard nothing.

Meena Raghunathan, Customer Success Director, Asia-Pacific and Middle East, Singapore. Raghunathan owns Zawiya and has absorbed every Dubai escalation personally. She wants a hard release train, a weekly client note that is actually true, and a quarter-end freeze respected by every pod including Pune. Much of her variable pay rides on the renewal. She is not saying that in August, under pressure in a Dubai meeting, she committed to a January date for the NHCX submission flow that no engineering lead has ever agreed to.

Vikram Sethi, Head of Enterprise Sales, North America, New Jersey. Sethi is chasing a US payer pilot worth roughly ₹14 crore in year one and wants a predictable quarterly release train for his proposal. His incentive is quota. He is not saying that the pilot's security questionnaire demands a SOC 2 Type II report and US data residency — work that would consume most of the platform pod for the same quarter as NHCX.

Sushmita Nair, Head of Regulatory Affairs, Mumbai. Nair holds that the NHCX target and the DPDP consent-manager obligations are not negotiable and must be sequenced first. Her incentive is a clean regulatory record. She is not saying that the consent-manager work was descoped in a June retrospective she did not attend, that the decision was never minuted, and that she learned of it in August.

You did not remove the critique. You moved it into a meeting where nobody has ninety minutes and the only thing on screen is a chart. That is a different thing from removing it, but the effect on the work is the same.

Ashwin Kurup, leadership meeting, 9 September 2026

I hear four pods, three calendars and a clause. What I need to hear is that NHCX ships and Dubai renews. Fix the cadence, but fix it by Monday, because on Thursday I am not standing in front of that board to talk about meetings.

7. The options, as Menon has written them down

A. Standardise and enforce. One cadence for the whole company, attendance tracked and written into every lead's objectives. Ramanathan has drafted the memo. The obstacle is legal as much as cultural: counsel advises that a mandated cadence would be arguable grounds for an earn-out dispute worth up to ₹47 crore, and Kurup will not authorise that six weeks before diligence. Menon has noted in the margin that enforcement would raise Thursday attendance to nearly a hundred per cent without changing a single thing anyone says.

B. Federate. Accept four cadences and keep two obligations in common: a written Thursday release declaration from each pod by 12:00 IST, and a monthly review where the numbers are argued rather than read. This is close to what has already happened without anyone deciding it — evidence either that it is the natural equilibrium or that it is how the company got here. Raghunathan's objection is precise: a declaration is only as good as the environment it describes, and nineteen weeks suggest nobody has been checking.

C. Sequence around the deadline. Freeze cadence changes until NHCX ships, appoint one delivery owner across all four pods with authority over the release calendar for that scope only, and revisit in April 2027 when the autonomy clause lapses. Sethi likes it because it gives him a date to sell; Nair because it puts regulatory work first. It leaves Zawiya's renewal, due 31 December, inside the freeze.

D. Change what the rhythm looks at. Keep the calendar, retire the dashboard, rebuild the weekly metric around customer-visible failure — claims not submitted in window, Sev-1s raised by customers, credits accrued — and give Sarkar the pen. Menon finds this the most honest of the four and the least sufficient. It corrects the instrument. It does not explain why, when Sarkar posted the truth about the instrument in June, nobody replied; nor why a descoping decision that mattered to the company's regulatory exposure was taken in a retrospective that produced no minutes and included nobody from Mumbai.

All four options describe a calendar. At the bottom of the page, in a hand she would not want photographed, Menon has written: Is the question which meetings we hold, or what a person can say in them, and whether anyone must answer? She has not decided whether that is insight or an excuse for having no plan.

8. The deadline and the constraints

The constraints do not arrange themselves neatly. Monday's all-hands is in nine hours; Thursday's board meeting needs a written delivery section that either repeats the July claim or corrects it. The autonomy clause runs to 31 March 2027. Zawiya's renewal is due by 31 December, and its freeze covers ten working days either side of the quarterly release window — in December, the last clear fortnight before the NHCX target. The 1 January date is not a statute, but Nair's view is that being visibly late would damage Kadalundi with precisely the payers it needs. The DPDP consent-manager work has no date at all.

Money constrains the rest. Payroll runs at ₹3.1 crore a month against ₹61 crore of cash and a round opening diligence in four weeks. Fourteen approved roles are unfilled and Kurup has not moved the hiring freeze. Credits of ₹75 lakh have accrued against a ₹1.44 crore cap, and Zawiya's counsel has written about the cap in terms finance has not yet answered. Three of the nine people outside India have resigned since May and have not been replaced. Sarkar's interview is on the twenty-second. Dandekar's earn-out vests in twenty-eight weeks, and eleven of his engineers vest with him.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Reading Exhibits 3 and 4 together, what did the weekly rhythm actually change between January and August 2026, and what did it only appear to change? Which exhibit would you trust, and what would you need to see to decide?
  2. Exhibit 5 shows Pune at 41 per cent attendance at the Thursday review, 93 per cent at its own Tuesday planning, and the highest engagement score of any large site. What is the naive reading of that row, and what is the defensible one?
  3. The rhythm was designed against one specific failure: three people who knew a change was risky and had nowhere to say so. Trace each ceremony to the failure it was meant to prevent. Which, as practised, still performs that function?
  4. All four options concern the shape of the calendar. What would a fifth look like if the diagnosis were not about the calendar at all, and what evidence here supports or undermines that diagnosis?
  5. The autonomy clause, the earn-out milestones, Ramanathan's promotion case, Raghunathan's variable pay and Kurup's fundraise all shape behaviour inside these meetings. Pick two and show concretely where the incentive surfaces in the record.
  6. It is Monday morning: a nine o'clock all-hands, a Thursday board meeting, a contested number in a pack she approved, a 1 January regulatory date, twenty-eight weeks until the autonomy clause lapses. What does Menon do on Monday, in what order and with whom — and what exactly does she tell the board about the 58 per cent?

10. After midnight

By half past one Menon had made two lists. The first was of people to reach before nine: Sarkar, because whatever he had seen she would rather hear at six than on Thursday; Dandekar, because a call asked for and not returned costs more than the call; Nair, because a descoped consent manager with no date becomes a regulator's question, not a product manager's. The second list was of things she could say at the all-hands. It had four entries, each a way of describing a calendar, and none a way of describing what had happened in June when a man in Toronto wrote down something true and the thread went quiet.

She thought about the November 2025 post-mortem that had started all of this, and the sentence she had underlined in it: the information existed in the building. It had existed again in May, in June, in August. The meetings had all been held. The dashboard had been green. Somewhere between the standup in Kochi and the committee in Dubai, the company had built an apparatus that ran every week without fail and reported, faithfully and on schedule, a version of itself that was no longer true. Whether the remedy was more of it, less of it, or something that was not an apparatus at all, Menon could not say at half past one, and the all-hands was at nine.

She closed the laptop, opened it again, and read the draft board memo once more without changing a word.

The Execution Rhythm at Neithal Fresh

Delivery & Technology: Delivery Process & Engineering Collaboration

On the morning of Monday, 14 September 2026, Aishwarya Balan stood at the glass wall of Neithal Fresh's engineering floor in the OMR IT corridor of Chennai, watching a dashboard trace live orders moving from dark stores in Sholinganallur, Velachery and Anna Nagar toward doorsteps across the city. Balan, Vice President of Product and Engineering, had four days. By six o'clock on Friday she owed the board a two-page section of the company's Diwali readiness plan titled, plainly, "Execution rhythm" — the cadence by which the 108-person product and engineering organisation would plan, build, review and learn through the eight weeks to Diwali, the busiest and most profitable stretch of Neithal Fresh's year. The board had asked for it after August's second missed release date in a row. Balan had spent the weekend re-reading three incident write-ups, a headcount chart, and a string of Slack messages from Berlin, Toronto and Singapore, and she still had not settled on an answer.

Neithal Fresh

Neithal Fresh was founded in Chennai in 2021 by two former Flipkart supply-chain engineers who bet that Tamil Nadu's dense, walkable neighbourhoods could support fifteen-minute grocery delivery the way Mumbai and Bengaluru already did. The company built a network of compact dark stores — forty of them by September 2026, across Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai, with a first Hyderabad cluster opening before Diwali — stocked with produce, dairy and daily essentials, and priced itself against Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit and Tata-owned BigBasket. Where Neithal Fresh had carved a niche was in fresh fish and coastal produce sourced directly from co-operatives near Ennore and Nagapattinam, a category the pan-India players handled poorly. On the back of that niche and a ₹340 crore Series B closed in early 2025, Neithal Fresh had begun licensing its dark-store fulfilment software, branded the Neithal Engine, to external retailers. Its first and largest licensee was Al Dana Hypermarkets, a fictional but sizeable grocery chain in Dubai, whose integration was managed out of Singapore and sold out of New Jersey. The mix of a fast-scaling consumer app and a young enterprise software line had pulled engineering headcount from 40 to 108 in eighteen months, spread across Chennai, Bengaluru, Pune, and single-person outposts in Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey.

The situation

Growth had outrun rhythm. In the company's first two years, cadence had simply meant whatever the sixteen-person team did each day: a standup in the Chennai office, a demo when something was ready, a retro when someone remembered to call one. That informality had scaled badly. By September 2026, four product pods — Checkout & Payments, Fulfilment & Dark Stores, Discovery & Search, and the Neithal Engine platform team — each ran its own version of agile ceremony. Checkout & Payments, led out of Bengaluru, had adopted textbook two-week Scrum sprints with sprint planning, daily standup, sprint review and retro. Fulfilment, based mostly in Chennai, shipped multiple times a day and had let its retro lapse after February; nobody could say when the last one had happened. The Neithal Engine platform team, coordinating Berlin design work, Toronto data science and the Dubai integration through Singapore, worked almost entirely asynchronously across time zones that overlapped for barely ninety minutes a day.

The cost of that patchwork showed up in Exhibit 1. A duplicated promo-code bug had recurred in March, six months after an earlier version of the same bug, because no retro had captured the original root cause. A payment-gateway conflict in August, during the Raksha Bandhan sales surge, had happened because Checkout & Payments and Fulfilment had each deployed changes to the same code path on the same afternoon with no shared release calendar between them. And in July, a version mismatch in the Neithal Engine's fulfilment API had breached Al Dana Hypermarkets' service-level agreement, because nobody had been sending Dubai a weekly note of what had changed. Farhan Mehta, the sales head who had closed the Al Dana account from his desk in New Jersey, forwarded that penalty notice to Balan with a single line: "This cannot happen again in Diwali week." Diwali fell on 8 November 2026; Neithal Fresh's order volumes typically ran five to six times normal in the surrounding fortnight, which meant any failure that occurred then would be both more likely, given the strain, and far costlier than an equivalent failure in a quiet month.

The people

Karthik Iyer, Engineering Manager for Checkout & Payments in Bengaluru, wanted the whole organisation to adopt his pod's disciplined two-week Scrum cycle. His team had the fewest defects of the four pods and he attributed this directly to the ceremony: nothing shipped that had not passed through planning, review and retro. He argued that a single, familiar cadence would make it easier to onboard the thirty engineers Neithal Fresh planned to hire before the Hyderabad launch.

Lena Fischer, Lead Product Designer for the Neithal Engine platform, worked from Berlin with a four-and-a-half-hour gap to Chennai and a nine-hour gap to Toronto. She resisted Karthik's proposal, pointing out that a two-week sprint calendar built around Indian working hours would push her sprint planning and review calls into her evenings twice a fortnight, on top of the daily syncs she already juggled. She wanted fewer live meetings and more written, asynchronous updates that she could read on her own schedule.

Arjun Nair, the data scientist who tracked delivery-time, defect and churn metrics from Toronto, had a narrower complaint: nobody looked at his weekly dashboard on a fixed schedule. Metrics were reviewed "when someone asked," which meant regressions sat unnoticed for two or three weeks at a time, as had happened with the March promo bug. He wanted a standing weekly slot where the numbers were actually discussed, not just published.

Ranjini Suresh, Customer Success Lead for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, worked from Singapore and owned the day-to-day relationship with Al Dana Hypermarkets. She was the one who had to explain the July SLA breach to Dubai, and she wanted a predictable, client-facing checkpoint — a short weekly note of what had shipped and what was coming — so that her next conversation with Al Dana would not begin with an apology.

What the numbers said

Balan asked her finance partner to cost out three candidate rhythms against the organisation's blended monthly payroll of roughly ₹2.48 crore across 108 people. Exhibit 2 shows what each option would consume in meeting time alone, before counting the incidents a thinner rhythm might fail to catch. It also shows something Karthik's argument had not fully reckoned with: Fulfilment and Checkout & Payments together already pushed seventeen to twenty-two production changes a week. A cadence built around a two-week sprint boundary would not slow that pace down so much as force it into an artificial box, with fixes for mid-sprint problems sometimes waiting a week or more to reach a formal review.

Exhibit 3: The proposed weekly rhythm (Option B)

A single daily 15-minute standup, always recorded for Berlin and Toronto; a Wednesday afternoon metrics check owned by Arjun Nair; a Friday release and review that doubles as the client-facing checkpoint Ranjini Suresh needs; and a retro every second Friday.

The options

Option A — Adopt Karthik's full Scrum cadence, organisation-wide. Every pod moves to two-week sprints with formal planning, daily standup, sprint review and retro, matching the practice behind Checkout & Payments' clean record. The upside is a single, familiar rhythm, easy to explain to new hires and to the board, with retro and review built into every cycle. The cost is real: Exhibit 2's ₹37.3 lakh a month is the highest of the three, sprint boundaries sit awkwardly against Fulfilment's daily shipping pace, and Lena Fischer's planning calls would routinely fall in her evening. It also risks becoming what distributed-team reports warn against — ceremony performed for its own sake rather than because the team needs it that week.

Option B — Establish one lightweight weekly rhythm. A daily fifteen-minute standup, recorded for those outside India's working hours; a Wednesday metrics check that Arjun Nair owns, surfacing regressions within days rather than weeks; a Friday release and review that doubles as the note Ranjini Suresh needs for Al Dana Hypermarkets; and a retro every second Friday, rotated between pods so one team's lesson reaches the others. The upside is that it addresses precisely the two gaps Exhibit 1 shows — a missing shared release checkpoint and a missing retro habit — at ₹22.4 lakh a month, roughly 40% less than Option A. The cost is discipline: pod leads must protect the Wednesday and Friday slots, and Karthik's team must give up part of a cadence it believes in.

Option C — Move to continuous flow with async-only check-ins. Drop fixed meetings almost entirely; rely on Slack updates and live dashboards, letting each pod self-manage. The upside is the lowest ceremony cost on paper, at ₹7.5 lakh a month, and the least strain on Lena's and Arjun's calendars. The cost is that this is close to what Fulfilment and the platform team were already doing when the March, August and July incidents happened: with no fixed weekly checkpoint, nothing forces a conflicting release to surface before it ships, and nothing forces a retro to happen at all. Adopting it organisation-wide going into the highest-traffic ten days of the year would formalise the very gap the incident log blames.

Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 show about the actual cause of Neithal Fresh's three incidents — was it a shortage of daily standups, or something else?
  2. How should Balan weigh Karthik Iyer's argument for uniform discipline against Lena Fischer's argument for protecting distributed colleagues' time?
  3. Using Exhibit 2, what does each option cost in a normal month, and why might that comparison understate the real difference between them during the Diwali fortnight?
  4. What is the smallest set of ceremonies — standup, review, retro, metrics check — that a team spread across five time zones needs to keep shipping without lapsing into ceremony for its own sake?

A note for the learner

The topic this case teaches is the execution rhythm: the weekly cadence of standups, reviews, retros and a metrics check that keeps a team's work visible to itself as it ships. It builds directly on agile ceremony in general, but it asks a sharper question than "is the team doing Scrum?" — it asks whether the specific cadence in place actually catches the specific failures a team is prone to. Exhibit 1 is the evidence a good answer must use: none of the three incidents traces to a missing daily standup, which all three pods already held in some form. Each traces to the absence of a weekly moment where releases were compared across pods, or where a defect's lesson was written down before the team moved on.

That evidence points toward Option B as the defensible path, not because its ₹22.4 lakh monthly cost is the deciding number by itself, but because it is the only option built around the checkpoints the incident log calls for: a Wednesday metrics check that would have caught March's regression within days, and a Friday release review that would have caught August's conflicting deploys and given Ranjini Suresh the client-facing note July's incident shows she needs. Option A adds real discipline but boxes a team that already ships daily into a two-week planning cycle it does not need, at the highest cost of the three and real friction for colleagues outside Indian hours. Option C is cheapest exactly where the company can least afford to be cheap: it removes the shared checkpoints without which March, August and July all happened, on the eve of the fortnight when a repeat would be costliest. A strong answer ties the choice back to what Exhibit 1 shows was actually missing, and explains why a rhythm sized to a growing but still young team beats either the heaviest or the lightest option on offer.

The Execution Rhythm

Standups, reviews, retrospectives and the weekly metric check, treated as an economic design problem rather than a set of ceremonies to be observed.

Section OneTwo companies, one week in March

On Tuesday, 3 March 2026, Devika Sundaram, VP of Product at Sangati Rides, was looking at a chart she had not asked for. Sangati Rides is a seven-year-old intercity travel app headquartered in Indiranagar, Bengaluru: bus seats, shared cabs and last-mile connections across roughly 380 routes in south and western India, 2.8 million monthly riders, ninety-six engineers in fourteen squads. The chart, built by her staff engineer Nithya Balasubramanian, plotted production deployments by day of the fortnight. It had two towers. Forty-one per cent of all deployments in the previous quarter had landed on the last two days of a sprint. Sangati's change failure rate on those two days was 9.1 per cent; on every other day it was 2.4 per cent.

The monsoon booking surge begins in earnest in the second week of June, and Sangati's revenue is seasonal enough that a two-day outage in that window costs more than most quarters of engineering. Devika's question was whether to abolish the fortnightly sprint altogether — move to continuous flow with a work-in-progress cap, keep the weekly metric review, and let releases happen whenever a change was ready. Her head of engineering, Karan Mehrotra, thought this would dissolve the last mechanism that made the roadmap predictable to the commercial team. Sangati's supply operations lead in Pune and a four-person data-platform team in Kraków would have to live with whatever she chose.

Two days later and 570 kilometres north, Rohit Deshmukh had the mirror-image problem. Rohit is Director of Product at Ahilya Grid Systems, a Hyderabad company that sells billing, outage-management and metering software to state electricity distribution companies — the DISCOMs — with a delivery centre in Nagpur and two site engineers permanently stationed with customers. Sixty-two engineers, ₹138 crore of annual revenue, and a constraint that Sangati has never had to think about: Ahilya's customers accept production changes only inside a monthly change window, agreed in advance with the customer's change advisory board, typically the second Saturday night of each month. A tariff order from a state electricity regulatory commission had fixed 30 June as the date by which a revised slab-billing engine had to be live in three states.

Ahilya's squads ran two-week sprints. Rohit's squad leads had begun campaigning to lengthen them to four weeks to match the release window. Their argument was that a two-week sprint that cannot release is theatre: the team declares work "done", it sits in staging for a fortnight, and half of it comes back with defects found during the pre-window regression. Rohit's retrospectives had, by his own audit, produced eleven action items in six months of which two had been completed.

Devika wanted to remove a cadence. Rohit wanted to lengthen one. Both of them were, in fact, facing the same question in different clothes, and the answer turns on a distinction neither of them had yet made explicit.

Section TwoThe idea, and the schools that disagree about it

An execution rhythm is the fixed, repeating schedule of recurring events and checks by which a delivery team coordinates, inspects and adapts — conventionally a daily standup, a periodic review or demo, a periodic retrospective, and a weekly review of the operating metric the team is accountable for. The functional definition matters more than the list: a rhythm is the set of moments at which information that is distributed across people is deliberately made common, plus the schedule that makes those moments free of negotiation.

The problem it was invented to solve is coordination under uncertainty. In plan-driven development, coordination is handled once, up front, by a schedule; when requirements move, the schedule is wrong and nobody notices for months. The iterative traditions replaced a single large act of coordination with many small ones. Scrum, presented by Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber at OOPSLA in 1995 and drawing its metaphor from Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka's 1986 Harvard Business Review paper, supplied the sprint, the review and the retrospective. Extreme Programming, developed by Kent Beck on the Chrysler C3 project between 1996 and 1999, supplied the daily stand-up and the practice of continuous integration that gives the review something real to show. The Agile Manifesto at Snowbird in February 2001 blended them into a movement. The weekly metric check has an entirely separate lineage in operating-review practice — Andrew Grove's High Output Management (1983), and the weekly business review as practised at Intel and later Amazon — and this disjoint ancestry is the source of several of the confusions treated below.

Four schools now disagree, in ways that matter for Devika and Rohit. It is worth stating each as a proposition its adherents would sign, and one they would not.

Four positions, and what each will and will not endorse
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Timeboxed iteration
Sutherland, Schwaber; Scrum orthodoxy		 A fixed-length iteration with a team commitment is the forcing function that makes finishing more attractive than starting, and makes estimates honest by exposing them fortnightly. That the length of the iteration should vary with the nature of the work, or that commitment can be dropped without losing the mechanism.
Flow / Kanban
David Anderson (2010); Donald Reinertsen (2009)		 The iteration boundary is itself a batch, and batches carry delay cost; cap work in progress, measure cycle time, and decouple the cadences of planning, review and release. That a fortnightly commitment improves predictability — they would say it improves only the appearance of predictability.
Operating review
Grove (1983); weekly business review practice		 The cadence that decides outcomes is the one at which operating metrics are reviewed by people who can act on them; delivery ceremonies are subordinate instruments. That a team retrospective is the primary engine of organisational improvement.
Empirical / DORA
Forsgren, Humble, Kim, Accelerate (2018)		 Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service are measurable and predict organisational performance; judge any ritual by its effect on those four. That velocity or story points measure anything about performance, or that any particular ceremony is necessary.

A fifth position deserves mention because it is increasingly common in product organisations: the Shape Up school, from Ryan Singer's 2019 book describing Basecamp's practice, which argues that a fortnight is too short to produce anything of consequence and proposes six-week cycles with a two-week cooldown, fixed time and variable scope, and no standup at all. It would sign "the team should be given a fixed appetite and allowed to cut scope to fit"; it would not sign "the team should commit to a defined scope."

The argument this page will build is that these schools are less in conflict than they appear, because three of them are arguing about different cadences. Once planning cadence, review cadence and release cadence are separated, most of the heat goes out of the dispute — and the residue that remains is a genuine disagreement, stated honestly in Section Ten.

Section ThreeMechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

Expert practitioners design a rhythm the way an operations manager designs a production line: by reasoning about batches, queues and transaction costs. Three pieces of formal apparatus do most of the work.

Little's Law, and why work-in-progress caps are the first lever

Little's Law states that for a stable system, average work in progress equals average throughput multiplied by average cycle time: WIP = λ × W. Rearranged, cycle time equals WIP divided by throughput. Take Sangati's Squad Kaveri — eight people working on the seat-selection and fare-display surface. In the quarter Devika was examining, the squad had an average of 13.6 items in progress at any moment and completed on average 7.2 items a week. Cycle time is therefore 13.6 ÷ 7.2 = 1.89 weeks, or 9.4 working days, which matched the tracker's measured median of 9 days almost exactly.

The instructive part is what the law implies. Throughput is hard to change — it is a function of skill, architecture and the size of items. WIP is trivially changeable: it is a policy. If Squad Kaveri caps concurrent items at 6, and throughput holds, cycle time falls to 6 ÷ 7.2 = 0.83 weeks, about 4.2 days. In practice throughput usually rises when WIP falls, because context-switching and waiting-for-review time both decrease. Nithya's experiment on two squads in January produced exactly that: WIP capped at 6, throughput rose to 7.9 a week, cycle time landed at 4.1 days.

Batch-size economics, and the shape of the curve

Donald Reinertsen's The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) frames release cadence as a batch-size problem. The total cost of operating at a given batch size is the sum of two opposing terms. Transaction cost is the fixed cost incurred per batch regardless of its size: at Ahilya Grid, a production release costs a full regression suite run with manual verification on three DISCOM configurations, a change advisory board submission, a rollback rehearsal and a site engineer on standby — measured by Rohit's team at 22 engineer-hours plus ₹40,000 of third-party testing per release. Holding cost is the cost of value sitting undelivered: it rises with batch size because the average item waits half the batch interval.

The practical consequence for Rohit is the one his squad leads had missed. Because the curve is flat near its minimum, arguing about whether the sprint should be two weeks or four weeks is arguing inside the flat part — it barely matters. What matters is the 22-hour transaction cost, because reducing it moves the whole optimum leftwards and cheaply. Automating the DISCOM configuration regression from 14 manual hours to 2 automated hours does more for Ahilya than any change of sprint length.

Queueing, and the second-order effect nobody plans for

The third piece of apparatus is elementary queueing. For a single-server queue, expected waiting time scales with ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) where ρ is utilisation. At 50 per cent utilisation the queue term is 1.0; at 80 per cent it is 4.0; at 90 per cent it is 9.0. This is the mathematics behind a fact every experienced engineering leader knows and almost no capacity plan reflects: a team planned to 95 per cent of capacity does not deliver 95 per cent as much as a team planned to 70 per cent, it delivers less, because everything waits behind everything else. A rhythm that consumes 17 per cent of capacity in recurring events and then plans the remaining 83 per cent to the hilt has created a queueing disaster and will blame the ceremonies for it.

Four second-order effects follow from the mechanics and are worth naming because practitioners routinely leave them implicit. First, a sprint boundary manufactures a deployment spike, which is precisely Devika's chart: batching releases to a boundary concentrates risk, and change failure rate rises with the number of changes released together. Second, a commitment manufactures scope-shaving: when a team must hit a fortnightly commitment, the variable it can move fastest is quality of the last item, and it will move it. Third, a standup creates an implicit service-level agreement on blocked work of roughly 24 hours; removing the standup without an explicit replacement silently changes that SLA, which is what makes the decision to remove it more consequential than it looks. Fourth, the value of a demo is the integration it forces, not the audience it attracts: the discipline of having something that runs end-to-end on a known date is the mechanism; the spectators are a side effect.

Section FourWhen the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The following four claims are testable in the sense that a team can gather the data in a fortnight and know whether the claim holds for it.

Four claims, each tested against both protagonists
ClaimSangati RidesAhilya Grid Systems
C1. A fixed cadence pays when the cost of deciding when to coordinate exceeds the cost of the coordination itself. Holds. Fourteen squads with cross-dependencies; ad-hoc coordination would consume the calendar. Holds strongly. A monthly external change board makes the coordination date non-negotiable anyway.
C2. A timeboxed commitment improves predictability only when item-size variance is low relative to the timebox. Test: coefficient of variation of item cycle time. Fails. Measured CV = 1.41. Items range from 2 hours to 6 weeks; a fortnightly commitment is a coin toss dressed as a plan. Holds. Measured CV = 0.62, because regulatory scope is specified in advance and items are comparable.
C3. A review has value only when someone outside the squad can reject the work. Weak. Reviews are attended by the squad and a designer; nothing has been rejected in eleven sprints. Holds. A site engineer and a DISCOM operations lead attend and have rejected work four times in six months.
C4. A retrospective produces change only where the team controls the thing it wants to change. Holds for squad-level items; fails for platform dependencies. Fails. Nine of eleven action items concerned the customer change window, which no squad controls.

Read across the table and the two diagnoses separate cleanly. Sangati has a review nobody can fail and a commitment its own variance makes meaningless; the parts of its rhythm that are load-bearing are the standup and the weekly metric check, and the sprint container is largely decorative. Ahilya has a genuinely load-bearing review and a defensible commitment, and a retrospective that has been asking a team to fix something outside its authority for six months, which is not a process failure but an escalation failure.

There are also conditions under which rhythm thinking is actively misleading. The first is when velocity is read as productivity: because story points are a unit the team defines, velocity can be increased by redefining the unit, and any organisation that rewards it will get that. The second is when a rhythm is used as a substitute for architecture. A team blocked by a monolith that takes forty minutes to build will retrospect about build times every fortnight for two years; the retro is the wrong instrument because the problem needs capital, not conversation. The third is early-stage discovery, where the thing being iterated is the hypothesis rather than the software, and a fortnightly delivery commitment actively discourages the abandonment that good discovery requires.

Section FiveHard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

The textbook rhythm assumes a single co-located cross-functional team owning one deployable product. Five situations break that assumption, and the way mature organisations handle them differs sharply from the way they describe themselves handling them.

Regulated and governed release environments. Ahilya's case is the canonical one: development can be continuous, but release is controlled by someone outside the company. The naive response — lengthen the sprint to match the window — couples the two cadences and imports the external constraint into everything the team does. What mature vendors actually do is decouple: a short development and review cadence feeding a staging environment that mirrors a named customer's configuration, a "release train" that departs on the window date carrying whatever is ready, and a separately owned hardening cadence in the week before the window. The same pattern appears in banking software governed by RBI change-management expectations and in health systems under state-level procurement rules.

Hardware plus software. Firmware and cloud have different natural cycle times, sometimes by an order of magnitude, because firmware carries build, flash, environmental test and certification steps that no amount of process design removes. Forcing a common cadence on both does not synchronise them; it makes the slower one fail publicly every iteration. Section Eight's third worked example is exactly this failure.

Two-sided marketplaces. Sangati has a supply side (bus operators and driver-partners, managed from Pune) and a demand side (riders). The specific rhythm requirement is that the weekly metric check must carry both sides in the same session. A rhythm that reviews rider conversion on Tuesday and operator payout health on Thursday produces, reliably, a team that optimises conversion into a supply shortage on the Mumbai–Pune corridor and does not find out for five weeks.

AI-native products. Here the rhythm faces a genuinely new problem, and the field has not settled it. In conventional software, if nothing is deployed, nothing changes. In a product with a model in the loop, behaviour can change without any deployment at all — a provider updates a model, a retrieval index drifts, the input distribution shifts. This breaks the implicit contract of the metric check, which is that movement in the number is caused by something the team did. Teams that handle this well add two things to the rhythm: a scheduled offline evaluation run against a fixed test set, treated as a first-class agenda item, and an explicit "what changed that we did not change" line in the weekly check. Teams that handle it badly discover a three-week-old regression through a customer complaint.

Organisational seams. The hardest case is not inside a team but between teams. Sangati's fourteen squads depend on a shared payments platform team and the Kraków data-platform team. Every organisation claims its squads are independent; almost none are. What actually works, in Devika's experience and in most large product organisations, is a lightweight dependency register — a single list of cross-team commitments with a requesting team, a providing team, a date and a named person — reviewed at a fortnightly seam meeting that exists for nothing else. What does not work is scaling the ceremony: a "scrum of scrums" attended by fourteen representatives, each reporting status, reproduces at organisation level the status-report failure mode that ruins standups at team level.

Section SixNine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Cadence and commitment are separable, and experts separate them

The competent practitioner treats "two-week sprint" as one atomic object: a fixed length, a planning session, a scope commitment, a review and a release, all bound together. The expert sees five independent design choices and varies them separately. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a team that says "our sprint" when it means, in different sentences, the planning interval, the review interval and the release interval. The obvious reading — that a team saying this is simply being loose with language — is wrong, because the conflation is causal: teams that use one word invariably change all three together when only one needed changing.

2. Standup duration is a thermometer, not a dial

When standups run long, the competent response is to shorten them by decree. The expert reads length as a symptom. A standup that has grown from eleven to twenty-six minutes is usually telling you either that work in progress has risen (more items to report), or that a dependency has appeared that nobody owns, or that the team has stopped trusting a written source of truth and is using the standup as a substitute for it. The tell is that the length rose gradually over six to eight weeks rather than jumping. Capping the meeting suppresses the signal and leaves the cause.

3. The review's value is the integration deadline, not the audience

Experts recognise a hollow review by a single detail: the demo is given from a feature branch or a local machine. When that happens, the forcing function has been removed — the team has produced a demonstration rather than an integration — and the review's remaining function is theatre. The obvious reading, that the problem is low attendance, is wrong; a well-attended demo from a branch is worse than a sparsely attended demo from staging.

4. Velocity is a capacity-planning input and nothing else

Story points measure relative size in a unit the team itself defines, which makes velocity useful for the team's own forecasting and useless for comparison across teams or over long periods. The expert's tell is directional: the moment velocity is quoted upward in an organisation, the unit begins to inflate, usually within two quarters, and it happens without anyone deciding to cheat. The obvious reading — that this is a discipline problem — is wrong. It is a measurement-design problem, and the fix is to stop reporting the number, not to police it.

5. "Too early to tell" is the hardest sentence in the metric check

Most weekly metric reviews are underpowered: the weekly variance of the number exceeds the effect size of anything shipped that week. The expert behaviour is to state, in advance, how long a change needs to run before its effect is readable, and then to record "too early to tell" without embarrassment for the intervening weeks. The tell that a team lacks this discipline is narrative whiplash — a hypothesis adopted one week and abandoned the next, each time with perfect confidence.

6. Retro items outside the team's control must be escalated, not re-discussed

Rohit's eleven action items are the canonical pathology. When a team surfaces a constraint it cannot move, the correct output is not an action item but a named escalation with an executive owner and a date, recorded in the retro and carried forward until it closes. The tell is repetition: the same item appearing in three consecutive retros without anyone outside the team ever being named. The obvious reading, that the team lacks follow-through, is precisely backwards — the team has excellent follow-through on an object it cannot reach.

7. Coordination cost scales with decision rights, not headcount

The pairwise-channel formula, n(n−1)/2, is the usual justification for small teams, and it is the wrong model. What actually drives coordination load is the number of people whose agreement is required before work can move. A nine-person squad with two clear technical decision-makers costs less to coordinate than a five-person squad operating by consensus. The expert's first question when a rhythm feels heavy is therefore never "how many people are in this meeting" but "who has to agree before this moves."

8. Protected time is part of the rhythm, and the only part with no invite

Because a rhythm is visible on a calendar and protected time is not, process design overwhelmingly optimises the meetings and ignores the negative space. Experts design the silence explicitly, usually as a two-hour block defended at organisation level, and they measure it: the count of uninterrupted blocks of 90 minutes or more per engineer per day is a cheap, honest metric that almost nobody tracks. The tell that a team has not done this is a calendar with recurring events at 11:00 and 15:00 — times chosen for convenience, which maximise fragmentation.

9. A rhythm that evaporates during an incident was never a rhythm

The real test of an execution rhythm is the fortnight in which a severity-one incident consumes four days. Competent teams suspend everything; experts suspend planning and refinement, keep the standup (now the coordination instrument that matters most), keep the metric check because the incident has changed the numbers, and defer the retrospective by exactly one cycle rather than skipping it. The tell of a fragile rhythm is that it resumes with no reference to the incident at all, as though the fortnight had not happened.

Section SevenAcross product types and company stages

Some of the variation across product types is real and some of it is folklore, and it is worth being plain about which is which. The genuine differences are three. In consumer products with continuous deployment, the weekly metric check is the load-bearing event because it is where experiments are called; the review is near-ceremonial. In B2B and enterprise, the review is load-bearing because an external party can reject the work, and the metric signals are slow enough that a weekly reading of renewal or expansion is noise — which is why good enterprise teams read leading indicators instead, as Ahilya does with meter-read completeness and billing-exception counts. In marketplaces and platforms, the structural requirement is that both sides appear in the same check, and that platform teams run a review whose audience is the consuming teams rather than customers.

In hardware and physical goods the difference is not one of emphasis but of arithmetic: cycle times differ by an order of magnitude across disciplines and no common cadence exists. In AI products the difference is the one described in Section Five — the metric check must account for change the team did not cause — plus a second: evaluation cadence becomes a first-class rhythm element alongside the four classical ones, because a model change with no code change can regress a product overnight.

Where the difference is not real, and where a great deal of consulting revenue is nonetheless earned, is in the daily standup. The coordination question a standup answers — what is blocked between now and tomorrow — is essentially identical in a consumer app, an enterprise billing system and a robotics company. The stylised claim that B2B teams "need more process" does not survive contact with the data; what B2B teams need is a review with real rejection authority, which is a different thing.

Stage changes the shape more than product type does. Below roughly twelve people in one room, most of the rhythm is redundant because coordination is ambient, and the right design is one weekly working session plus an honest metric check. Between twelve and sixty, the classical four-event rhythm is close to optimal and the main failure is ceremony inflation. Above sixty, the rhythm must nest, and the nesting rule is arithmetic: outer cadences must be integer multiples of inner ones, or teams spend their working lives preparing for reviews that land mid-cycle. Sangati's fourteen squads run a weekly inner cadence, a fortnightly seam meeting and a six-weekly portfolio review — 1, 2 and 6, all integer multiples — and the arithmetic is the reason the calendar does not collide.

Section EightThree worked examples

Example one: Sangati Rides decouples release from sprint

Nithya's January experiment ran on two of fourteen squads for six weeks. The intervention was narrow: cap concurrent items at six, remove the end-of-sprint release freeze, keep the standup, keep planning weekly, replace the fortnightly demo with a weekly session combining demo and metric check.

Sangati Rides: two squads before and after, six weeks
MeasureBeforeAfterChange
Average WIP (items)13.66.0−56%
Throughput (items/week)7.27.9+10%
Median cycle time (working days)9.44.1−56%

Recurring-event hours per person per fortnight12.58.0−36%

The change-failure-rate result is the counter-intuitive one and deserves the explanation. Deploying three times as often did not make failures three times as likely; it made each deployment smaller, so that when something broke the search space was one change rather than eleven, which is also why time to restore more than halved. This is the central empirical finding of the DORA research programme, and Sangati reproduced it in six weeks on eighteen people.

Example two: Ahilya Grid attacks transaction cost instead of sprint length

Rohit did the arithmetic his squad leads had not. A production release cost 22 engineer-hours: 14 hours of manual regression across three DISCOM configurations, 3 hours of change-advisory-board documentation, 2 hours of rollback rehearsal, 3 hours of site-engineer standby. At ₹2,100 per engineer-hour that is ₹46,200, plus ₹40,000 of third-party security testing, so ₹86,200 per release. Twelve releases a year is ₹10.3 lakh.

Lengthening the sprint from two weeks to four weeks would have saved six planning sessions, six reviews and six retrospectives a year across four squads — roughly 4 hours × 3 events × 6 × 4 squads × 8 people, or 2,304 person-hours, about ₹48 lakh. That is a real number, which is why the proposal was attractive. Against it: item cycle time would have risen, because a four-week planning horizon means the median item waits two weeks rather than one before being picked up, and Ahilya's own data showed defect-discovery latency rising with staging age at roughly 0.4 additional defects per item per extra week in staging.

The alternative Rohit priced was automating the configuration regression: about 340 engineer-hours of investment, roughly ₹7.1 lakh, reducing the 14 manual hours to 2. That takes the per-release transaction cost from 22 hours to 10, saves ₹3.0 lakh a year in direct cost, and — far more importantly — makes a fortnightly release to a willing customer's pre-production environment economic for the first time, which is what actually moves defect discovery earlier. Payback on the automation is 28 months on direct cost alone and about seven months once the defect-latency effect is included at Ahilya's measured rework cost of ₹18,000 per late-discovered defect.

Example three: where it failed — Kartavya Instruments

Kartavya Instruments, in Coimbatore, builds industrial vibration-monitoring instruments: a sensor unit with embedded firmware, a gateway, and a cloud analytics service. In April 2025 a newly hired engineering director imposed a single two-week sprint cadence across all three disciplines, with a common sprint review, a common retrospective and a shared velocity chart.

Kartavya Instruments: the cost of one cadence imposed on three cycle times

The mechanism of failure is visible in the first column. Firmware items had a median cycle time of 31 days because a change required a build, a flash onto hardware, a 72-hour thermal soak test and, for anything touching the safety path, a re-certification submission. A two-week commitment on a 31-day item is not ambitious; it is arithmetically impossible. The firmware team therefore failed publicly in seven of eight sprints, in front of colleagues whose items took five days, and the shared retrospective became a forum in which the firmware engineers explained physics to people who heard excuses. Four of eleven firmware engineers left in five months. Kartavya's own estimate of the cost was ₹1.1 crore in recruitment, ramp-up and lost throughput, and an eleven-week slip to a product launch.

The recovery, begun in October 2025, was not a return to no process. Firmware moved to a four-week planning cadence with a milestone-based commitment rather than an item-based one; cloud stayed on a weekly cadence with a WIP cap; gateway adopted a fortnight. The three disciplines kept exactly two things in common: a single weekly metric check attended by all three leads, reading four product-level numbers rather than three sets of velocity; and a quarterly integration milestone on a fixed date at which all three had to produce a working end-to-end system. Velocity charts were deleted entirely. By March 2026 firmware attrition had stopped and the integration milestone had been hit twice consecutively. The lesson Kartavya's leadership drew, and stated in writing, was that synchronisation is required at integration points, not everywhere.

Section NineFailure modes, early warnings and the cost of catching them late

The pattern across all five is worth stating: every one of them has a cheap diagnostic available in a single afternoon, and every one of them is nevertheless usually discovered through a missed commitment months later. The reason is that rhythms degrade gradually and without an owner. Devika's practice — a calendar audit and a blocked-ageing measurement once a quarter, thirty minutes of analysis — is the cheapest insurance in the discipline, and it is rare.

Section TenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements survive careful analysis, and it would be dishonest to resolve them here.

Does a timebox with a commitment create real predictability, or only its appearance?

The timebox position, in its strongest form, is that a commitment creates a social object that people organise around: teams that commit finish things, teams that merely flow start things. The evidence is practical and widespread — two decades of teams whose delivery improved on adopting sprints — and the mechanism is psychological rather than mathematical. The flow position, at its strongest, is that this predictability is measured in a unit the team controls and therefore proves nothing, that Little's Law gives an honest forecast from cycle-time distributions without any commitment at all, and that the commitment's observable effect is scope-shaving at the boundary. For the timebox position to be wrong, teams that drop commitment while capping WIP should show no deterioration in on-time delivery of externally promised dates — Sangati's experiment is a small piece of evidence that they do not. For the flow position to be wrong, forecast accuracy from cycle-time distributions should degrade badly when item-size variance is high, which is exactly when teams most need forecasts. Both of those things appear to be true, which is why the argument persists.

Is the retrospective the engine of improvement, or a batching of something that should be continuous?

The Scrum position is that improvement requires a protected, blameless space that will not happen spontaneously under delivery pressure. The lean position, descending from Toyota practice and stated for software by Mary and Tom Poppendieck in 2003, is that batching improvement into a fortnightly meeting is itself the waste: a team that fixes things when it notices them does not need a scheduled forum, and the existence of the forum licenses people to defer. For the lean position to be wrong, teams without retrospectives should show fewer completed process changes — which is what most surveys find, though the causation is unclear because teams that abandon retros are often teams under pressure. For the Scrum position to be wrong, retro action completion rates should be high, and Rohit's two-of-eleven is depressingly typical.

Does a synchronous daily standup survive distributed work?

The synchronous position holds that blocked work needs a same-time, same-place-in-time forum because a blocker is a request and requests decay in writing. The asynchronous position, associated with fully distributed companies, holds that the standup is a legacy of colocation, that a written update is searchable, inclusive of people in other time zones and honest in a way that speech is not, and that what teams actually miss when they drop it is not the information but the ambient sense of each other. Sangati's Kraków team is the live test: at a four-and-a-half-hour time difference from Bengaluru the standup is affordable; at nine and a half hours it would not be. Nobody has good evidence about which mechanism dominates, and the honest answer is that the right design depends on overlap hours, which is a fact about geography, not about process.

Do delivery metrics measure the right thing at all?

The DORA position is that deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore are measurable, hard to game and predictive of organisational performance. The counter-position — held by many product leaders and implicit in the operating-review school — is that all four measure the pipe rather than what flows through it, that a team can achieve elite scores while shipping a product nobody wants, and that optimising them attracts exactly the organisations most inclined to substitute delivery metrics for product judgement. This is the disagreement with the highest stakes for a product manager, and it is the reason serious product curricula caution against teaching too much agile mechanics: the mechanics are learnable in a fortnight, and mastering them is entirely compatible with being wrong about what to build.

Section ElevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. First, they never say "sprint" without specifying which cadence they mean, and they will happily run planning weekly, review fortnightly and release continuously without feeling that anything is inconsistent. Second, they reach for a measurement before a meeting: confronted with "our process is broken," they ask for cycle-time distribution, blocked-work ageing, change failure rate and a count of uninterrupted blocks, and they can get all four from existing tools in an afternoon. Third, they treat ceremonies as expenditure with a return, and can state the return: this event buys us a 24-hour ceiling on blocked work, that one buys us an integration deadline, this one buys us a weekly honest reading of one number. Fourth, and most distinctively, they know what the rhythm cannot do. A flawless rhythm ships the wrong roadmap on time with high morale and clean charts. Mastery includes the discipline of not letting the visible competence of execution substitute for the invisible, unglamorous, much harder work of deciding what is worth executing.

The negative tell is equally diagnostic. Someone who has studied rather than internalised this will defend a ceremony on grounds of correctness — "retrospectives are part of Scrum" — rather than on grounds of what it buys, and will respond to a delivery problem by adding a meeting, because adding a meeting is the cheapest visible action available to anyone in an organisation.

Section TwelveWhat each of them decided

Devika did not abolish the sprint; she stopped using the word. On 17 March Sangati Rides moved to a weekly planning cadence, a weekly combined demo and metric check with both marketplace sides represented, a work-in-progress cap of six per squad, and continuous release with no freeze. The fortnightly retrospective survived unchanged, and a fortnightly seam meeting with a dependency register was added for the payments and data platforms. Her reasoning rested on the C2 test: with a coefficient of variation of 1.41 on item cycle time, the fortnightly commitment was not producing predictability, and the release freeze that came bundled with it was producing a measurable concentration of failure two days before the highest-revenue season of the year. She kept the standup, because the blocked-ageing argument was never in dispute.

Rohit rejected the four-week sprint. On 20 March Ahilya Grid Systems kept a weekly planning cadence and a fortnightly customer-attended review, funded 340 engineer-hours of regression automation, and made one change to the retrospective: any item the team does not control is converted immediately into a named escalation with an executive owner and a review date, and the first agenda item of every retro is reading out the open escalations. The revised slab-billing engine went live across three states in the June change window, six days before the regulator's deadline.

Three questions in the style of a teaching note.

1. Devika's decision rests on a coefficient of variation of 1.41. Suppose the figure had been 0.5. Which parts of her design should change, and which should not — and does the deployment-spike evidence survive the change?

2. Rohit converted uncontrollable retro items into named escalations. What are the second-order risks of that policy — for the team, for the executives named, and for the retrospective itself — and how would you know within one quarter whether it was working?

3. Kartavya Instruments kept exactly two things synchronised across three disciplines. If you were asked to apply that principle at Sangati Rides, with fourteen squads and two platform teams, what would the minimum shared synchronisation set be, and what would you deliberately leave unsynchronised?

Section ThirteenGoing deeper

Agile in practice. The rhythm is agile's ceremonies as a team actually lives them, and the parent topic supplies the intellectual history and the values behind the practices — which is what you need in order to argue about a ceremony without being accused of heresy.

Distributed and asynchronous teams. Everything on this page assumes enough overlapping hours for a same-time standup. Remove that assumption and the whole rhythm has to be redesigned from written artefacts outward; this is the single highest-value next topic for most readers.

Release management and launch readiness. The rhythm decides when work is done; release management decides when it is safe. Teams that conflate the two ship on cadence straight into an incident, which is exactly what Devika's chart of end-of-sprint change failures was showing.

Cross-functional rituals. The squad rhythm is only the inner loop. Marketing, support, sales and finance run cadences of their own, and the seams between them are where launches are actually lost.

The software development lifecycle. Supplies the stages the rhythm moves work through, and the vocabulary — staging, hardening, regression — that Sections Five and Eight lean on without defining.

Kanban and flow. The formal apparatus behind Section Three: work-in-progress limits, cumulative flow diagrams, cycle-time distributions and service-level expectations, which are what let a team forecast without committing.

Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing. Where the item-size variance that drove the C2 test comes from, and how to reduce it — the most reliable way to make a timebox work is to make items comparable.

Backlog management and refinement. The unglamorous work that makes planning short. Most rhythms that feel heavy are rhythms in which refinement is being done in the planning meeting with twice the audience.

Definition of done. Without a shared, testable definition, the review cannot reject anything, and claim C3 fails automatically — which is the mechanism behind Sangati's eleven consecutive reviews in which nothing was ever turned down.

The PM–engineering relationship. The substrate under all of it. A rhythm is a set of agreements about how two functions will share information, and no amount of ceremony design compensates for a product manager and a tech lead who do not trust each other's judgement.
